newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Skoda chairman dies in car crash.
newsitem.headline: Skoda chairman dies in car crash.

text.p: Skoda Auto a.s. chairman and chief executive Ludvik Kalma, the Czech face at a carmaker now dominated by Germans, died late Sunday in an accident while driving the new model he helped put on the market.
Kalma's Octavia sedan collided with a truck on a highway intersection close to the southern Czech city of Tabor, a compnay spokesman told Reuters on Monday. He was 55-years-old.
The Czech news agency CTK quoted local police as saying the driver of the cargo truck was charged with causing the accident after stopping in the intersection from a secondary road.
The truck driver's condition or that of other occupants, if any, was not disclosed.
It said Kalma's luxury model was equipped with dual front-seat airbags. He is the first person known to have died in an Octavia which went on sale earlier this month.
Kalma helped lead Skoda's post-Communist renaissance, moving to headquarters in Mlada Boleslav north of Prague in 1991 from managing a southern Czech car engine maker.
He was chosen to head Skoda as the Czech government sold a majority stake in the company to Volkswagen AG.

As the German car maker took over management, Kalma was surrounded by executives dispatched by VW's headquarters, but he remained the one Czech who spoke for the century-old company, especially to local media.

During Kalma's tenure, Skoda went from a symbol of East Bloc inefficiency and lack of imagination to a dynamic part of the Volkswagen group -- a company which Volkswagen chairman Ferdinand Piech once called "our most beautiful daughter."
Over the past two-years Skoda completed a gleeming new purpose-built plant in Mlada Boleslav to build the Octavia based on Volkswagen's Audi A3 and upgraded Golf model platform.
This autumn, Skoda unveiled the new mid-sized sedan which it hoped would put an end to the Communist-era jokes and make the heavily re-invested company finally profitable.
Kalma served as the Czech conduit to smooth over tough personnel changes made to boost efficiency.

"We have a very big task ahead of us. We must be competitive. We must markedly increase our productivity," Kalma told a news conference after the VW contract giving it 70 percent of Skoda stock was finalised in 1994.
Skoda's workforce dropped to about 17,000 from over 20,000 under Communism, as Volkswagen began instituting its strategy of on-site contractors to build some of Skoda's components.

The company says its production accounts for over 100,000 jobs in the Czech Republic, but the new factory actually left Skoda with a shortage of manpower, in a country with three percent unemployment.
Under Kalma, Skoda has avoided any major industrial action by its union workers, despite major changes to shift structures and assembly-line practices.
Skoda expects to break even or post a small profit this year, improving from a 1.6 billion czech crown ($59.75 million) loss in 1995.
Kalma, who served as vice-president of the Czech Confederation of Industry and Transportation, is survived by his wife two sons and a daughter.
Skoda and Volkswagen both declined comment on a possible successor.
($1=26.78 Czech Crown)
